Accordingly, the first vowel is stressed in words beginning in a consonant or cluster -- kápan short, ŋgóðRo black -- but the second vowel in words which begin in a vowel -- ayóŋ I, alán sky, aðá crow. (Hale 1966: 179) ... At all events, Liŋŋit̠iɣ and Alŋit̠ (Alngith) are dialects of a single language, sharing 87 percent of basic vocabulary. (Hale 1966: 176) ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the first vowel that is preceded by a consonant: on the first syllable of consonant-initial words, on the second syllable of vowel-initial words (the post-initial-dropping Northern Paman pattern; historically the etymological second syllable). Stated for Linngithigh; Hale treats Alngith as a co-dialect of the same language in the same source, so for Alngith this is a co-dialect inference, not a direct observation.
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned; stress described as fully predictable. Hale notes Linngithigh morphemes are predominantly monosyllabic and often begin in consonant clusters.
new_statements.domain_note: Word stress ('Word stress in Liŋŋit̠iɣ is predictable'), illustrated on isolated lexical items; pp.167-168 additionally give the diachronic Northern-Paman-wide shift of primary stress from the initial to the second syllable of Paman stems, which covers Alngith as a sampled variety.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted stress rule describes Linngithigh (Liŋŋit̠iɣ, Glottolog leni1238), not Alngith directly. Hale 1966 p.176 states in the same source that 'Liŋŋit̠iɣ and Alŋit̠ (Alngith) are dialects of a single language, sharing 87 percent of basic vocabulary' (Glottolog groups them as Linngithigh-Alngith, leni1237); Sutton & Hale 2021:117 repeat 'distinct but close dialects of a single language', and Wikipedia (citing Hale 1976a:14) reports identical sound inventories, Alngith differing by metathesis. Hale's own Alngith data are 3 leaves (AIATSIS MS 882 (12)). No Alngith-specific stress sentence was found in any opened source; the Alngith entry, if catalogued, should be flagged as a co-dialect inference from Linngithigh with the Northern-Paman-wide stress shift (Hale 1966:167-168) as the only group-level statement that names Alngith's group.

new_statements.identity_note: The only full stress statement held by the project (Hale 1966 p.179) is for Linngithigh (leni1238), which Hale calls a co-dialect of a single language with Alngith (87 percent shared basic vocabulary, p.176). Hale 1976a treats Alngith inside the Northern Paman group [Mpalitjanh, Alngith, Awngthim, Ntra'ngith, Mbiywom] and, per Wikipedia citing p.14, says Alngith and Linngithigh share the same sound inventory. No Alngith-specific stress sentence has been seen in any opened text.

new_statements.relation_note: Not in the catalog; compatible with the existing statements. The Hale 1966 Liŋŋitiɣ rule 'the first vowel which is preceded by a consonant is stressed' (fixed: other position) and the Hale 1976a snippets 'stress the first vowel that follows a consonant' / 'a prior shift of stress from the first to the second syllable' are the synchronic and diachronic faces of the same fact; Hale 1964 gives the diachronic face only (stress shifted to the second syllable of the proto-stem) and adds that stress is 'a strictly phonetic feature' (non-contrastive). It is a Northern-Paman-wide statement that explicitly includes Alngith in its sample but says nothing specific to Alngith and does not formulate the…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level and diachronic only: across the Northern Paman languages (13 samples including Alŋit/Alngith, p. 252) primary stress, which Hale calls 'a strictly phonetic feature' (i.e. non-contrastive), shifted from the initial to the second syllable of the Proto-Paman stem (*C2V2), and this shift accompanied and partly caused the loss of the initial consonant and the loss/reduction/metathesis of the first vowel. After that reduction the formerly second syllable is the first syllable with an onset consonant in the modern languages. The article gives no Alngith-specific synchronic stress rule and cites no Alngith forms (sections 2.1-2.7, pp. 258-261, exemplify from Liŋŋitiɣ, Uraði, Yinwum, Mpalityan, Awŋtim, Aritiŋŋitiɣ, Mbiywom).
new_statements.exceptions: none on stress. On the associated reduction: 'In all Northern Paman languages, except Uraði and its sister dialects, *C1 was lost invariably.. Short *V1 was lost in some languages, retained in others, and metathesized in still others. Long *V·1 was shortened in all.' (p. 256)
new_statements.identity_note: Hale 1964 treats Alŋit (Alngith) as one of 13 Northern Paman samples collected in 1960 from informants at Weipa and Aurukun Missions, subgroup (D) with Liŋŋitiɣ (p. 252). p. 253 locates Alŋit on the northeast side of the Embley River at the then site of Weipa Mission, across the Embley from Liŋŋitiɣ, and gives /layŋŋit/ (Laynngith, cp. /layn/ 'this') as an alternate designation, calling Liŋŋitiɣ 'closely similar'. The stress statement on p. 256 is about Northern Paman as a whole ('in Paman stems'), not about any one dialect; the cognate matrix (p. 262) gives Alŋit-Liŋŋitiɣ 87 shared items of 100.
